title: Changes in the library
passage:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome back after the holiday. I'd like to tell you about a few changes in the library this term.

First, the opening times. We now open at a quarter to eight every morning, fifteen minutes earlier than before, so you can come in and study before lessons. We still close at half past four, except on Fridays, when we close at three.

Second, the computers. The ten computers by the window are now for schoolwork only. If you want to play games or watch videos, please use the two computers next to the magazines, and only at lunchtime.

Third, borrowing books. You can now take out five books at a time instead of three, and you can keep them for three weeks. If you need a book for longer, just ask at the desk.

Finally, we're starting a reading club on Wednesday afternoons. This term we're reading mystery stories. If you'd like to join, write your name on the list by the door. Thank you, and enjoy the library.

title: The museum trip
passage:
Ms Patel: Leo, have you got a minute? It's about the trip to the science museum next Friday.
Leo: Yes, of course. Is it still happening?
Ms Patel: It is, but the coach company called this morning. They can't take us at eight o'clock any more, so we're leaving at half past nine instead.
Leo: That's actually good news. I live quite far away, so eight was always going to be difficult for me.
Ms Patel: I thought you might say that. The bad news is that we'll get back later, at about five, not four.
Leo: Will my mum need to pick me up, then? The last school bus goes at half past four.
Ms Patel: Yes, or you can walk to the station with Mr Green's group. He's taking the students who go home by train.
Leo: I'll ask my mum. And do we still need to bring lunch?
Ms Patel: No, that part has changed too. The museum café is giving every student a free sandwich and a drink, so just bring some money for the gift shop if you want.
Leo: Great. I'll tell the others.

title: A year without a phone
passage:
Interviewer: My guest today is Daniel Reyes, who spent a whole year without a smartphone. Daniel, what made you do it?
Daniel: Honestly, it started as a bet with my sister. She said I couldn't last a month. I was checking my phone about a hundred times a day, so I suppose she had a point.
Interviewer: And you lasted a year. What was the hardest part?
Daniel: Not the things I expected. I thought I'd miss social media, but after about two weeks I hardly thought about it. What I really missed were maps. I got lost a lot, especially in the first month, and I was late for nearly everything.
Interviewer: Did it change your relationships?
Daniel: In some ways, yes. A few friends stopped inviting me out, because it was harder to make plans with me. But the friends I did see, I paid more attention to. We actually talked, instead of all looking at our screens.
Interviewer: Would you recommend it?
Daniel: I wouldn't tell everyone to give up their phone completely. That isn't realistic for most people. But I'd suggest trying one phone-free day a week. That's what I do now, and it's made a real difference to how well I sleep.
